# Proposition 5
## Should successor elections be eliminated from recall elections of state officials?
When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.
## Yes Argument
California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.
In the unsuccessful 2021 recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom, the top replacement candidate received the support of just 28% of voters in the recall election — with millions of voters simply leaving the second question blank.
Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.
## No Argument
Proposition 5 takes away the ability of Californians to choose their leaders.
Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.
California’s recall system has worked well for more than a century and doesn’t need to be changed.

### Proposition 5
##### Recall Reform (2026)
California’s recall election process was designed as a democratic safeguard to hold corrupt or abusive officials accountable.
However, under current law, the recall ballot presents voters with two connected questions: **(1)** Should the official be recalled? and **(2)** If so, who should replace them?
These two questions together create a dangerous loophole.
An elected official can be removed by a narrow majority.
Then, a candidate listed in question #2 can win the office with far less than 50% of the votes cast in the election.
This encourages political actors to target officials they couldn’t defeat in a regular election and to install replacements who lack broad public support.
We saw this dynamic play out during the 2021 gubernatorial recall attempt.
Although voters overwhelmingly rejected the recall by nearly the exact margin as the original gubernatorial election, California taxpayers were forced to pay over **$200 million** for an unnecessary election.
Nearly 70% of California likely voters called the effort a waste of taxpayer money.
Had the recall succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with only about 28% support from recall voters.
Proposition 5 enacts a single, commonsense fix to restore fairness and integrity: **it removes the second question from state recall ballots.**

# Proposition 5
## Should successor elections be eliminated from recall elections of state officials?
When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.
## Yes Argument
California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.
In the unsuccessful 2021 recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom, the top replacement candidate received the support of just 28% of voters in the recall election — with millions of voters simply leaving the second question blank.
Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.
## No Argument
Proposition 5 takes away the ability of Californians to choose their leaders.
Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.
California’s recall system has worked well for more than a century and doesn’t need to be changed.

#### RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS
California’s recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official.
It should never become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a small fraction of voters.
However, that is exactly what today’s recall rules allow, since the same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets the most votes, even if that’s far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process.
Voters are asked to remove an officer by majority vote, then hand that same office to a replacement chosen by whomever gets the most votes, often in a field crowded with dozens of candidates and with no requirement that the winner reach half the vote.
That’s a loophole that can easily be exploited.
In 2021, had the recall against Governor Newsom succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with the support of just 28% of recall voters, a stark illustration of exactly this problem.
Prop 5 restores the recall to its proper purpose: deciding whether an official should remain in office.
It shuts down that back door with one clean fix: removing the replacement candidate vote from the recall ballot itself.
If a recall succeeds, the vacancy is filled through succession, appointment, or a later election decided by real majority support.
These are the same rules used to fill any other vacancy in state government.

### Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

As described below, Proposition 5 changes the recall process to make it like the existing process for filling vacant state offices, except for the process to recall the Governor.

As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.

### Summary
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

### What will the measure do?
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time.
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to nix that system by first asking voters to choose whether or not to oust an official.
Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date.

## Should successor elections be eliminated from recall elections of state officials?
When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.
## Yes Argument
California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.
In the unsuccessful 2021 recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom, the top replacement candidate received the support of just 28% of voters in the recall election — with millions of voters simply leaving the second question blank.
Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.
## No Argument
Proposition 5 takes away the ability of Californians to choose their leaders.
Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.
California’s recall system has worked well for more than a century and doesn’t need to be changed.

## Abstract
The California recall election of 2003 provides an excellent setting for investigating voter rationality and certain forms of sophisticated voting.
In a pre-election telephone survey, 1,500 registered voters were asked to make pairwise comparisons between the major candidates, and their responses were combined to infer preferences.
Individuals’ preference orderings over the major candidates rarely exhibited intransitivity.
The patterns of tactical voting observed in the replacement part of the recall election were consistent with the declining rate hypothesis.
Voters also engaged in ‘hedge voting’ on the recall question itself.
The results suggest that voters’ decisions are ‘rationalistic’: while voters are consistent in forming utility-based preference rankings and choosing on that basis, their voting strategies do not incorporate probability assessments in a realistic, consistent fashion, if at all.

#### RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS
California’s recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official.
It should never become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a small fraction of voters.
However, that is exactly what today’s recall rules allow, since the same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets the most votes, even if that’s far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process.

# Your last-minute guide to Proposition 5: Changing how recall elections work
## The basics
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time.
Proposition 5 breaks up that process into two parts, prioritizing the voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement.
## The impact
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to change the current recall system.
Under the proposed changes, voters would first be asked to choose whether or not to oust an official.
Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date.
In the case of a special election, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.

### The Recall Election
- Seven states hold recall elections simultaneously with election for a successor for most offices: Arizona, California, Colorado, Michigan, Nevada, North Dakota and Wisconsin.
- In five states, a recall election is followed by a separate special election for a successor for most state offices: Georgia, Illinois, Louisiana, Minnesota and Rhode Island (state legislature only).

# Proposition 5
## Should successor elections be eliminated from recall elections of state officials?
When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.
## Yes Argument
California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.
In the unsuccessful 2021 recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom, the top replacement candidate received the support of just 28% of voters in the recall election — with millions of voters simply leaving the second question blank.
Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.
## No Argument
Proposition 5 takes away the ability of Californians to choose their leaders.
Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.
California’s recall system has worked well for more than a century and doesn’t need to be changed.

# Proposition 5
## Should successor elections be eliminated from recall elections of state officials?
When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.
## Yes Argument
California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.
In the unsuccessful 2021 recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom, the top replacement candidate received the support of just 28% of voters in the recall election — with millions of voters simply leaving the second question blank.
Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.
## No Argument
Proposition 5 takes away the ability of Californians to choose their leaders.
Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.
California’s recall system has worked well for more than a century and doesn’t need to be changed.

One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials.
According to the Legislative Analyst's Office, the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement.
In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy.
In the case of a governor's recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting "yes" means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting "no" means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don't end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall.
With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it's the people's right to choose a governor's replacement.
They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.

### Summary

As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.

Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.

If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

## Should successor elections be eliminated from recall elections of state officials?
When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.
## Yes Argument
California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.
In the unsuccessful 2021 recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom, the top replacement candidate received the support of just 28% of voters in the recall election — with millions of voters simply leaving the second question blank.
Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.
## No Argument
Proposition 5 takes away the ability of Californians to choose their leaders.
Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.
California’s recall system has worked well for more than a century and doesn’t need to be changed.

### Background
***Recall of State Officials.*** The State Constitution allows voters to remove state officials from office before their term ends through a recall.

...

...

***Removes Second Question From Recall Elections.*** Proposition 5 removes the second question—who should replace a recalled official—from a recall election.
This means, in future recall elections, voters would only decide whether to remove an elected official from a state office, not who would replace the official.

# Your last-minute guide to Proposition 5: Changing how recall elections work
## The basics
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time.
Proposition 5 breaks up that process into two parts, prioritizing the voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement.
## The impact
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to change the current recall system.
Under the proposed changes, voters would first be asked to choose whether or not to oust an official.
Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date.
In the case of a special election, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.

# California's Recall Is Not Overpowered
## Abstract
The recall is one of three direct democracy tools in California.
Following the failed 2021 recall attempt against California Governor Gavin Newsom, the state recall process has been criticized for evolving beyond its intended purpose to the point of being overpowered and prone to abuse.
After reviewing the recall’s original intent, we conduct a quantitative analysis of state and local recall attempts in California and compare this to other recall states.
We conclude that the critique is unjustified.
In California and elsewhere, state official recalls are frequently attempted but rarely qualify for the ballot, demonstrating that the existing recall system is an effective filter.
We validate the charge that the recall is primarily a tool of out-party interests, but conclude that this is an intended design feature rather than an unanticipated defect.
We conclude instead that California’s local recall is the better target for reform efforts, given its comparatively easier qualifying requirements, greater use, and higher success rates.
Rather than deviating from its intended purpose, in its 110 years the California state official recall proved to be exactly what its Progressive designers intended: a voter weapon to menace and remove public officials, but one that is difficult to deploy.

## Should successor elections be eliminated from recall elections of state officials?
When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.

# California's Recall Is Not Overpowered
## Abstract
The recall is one of three direct democracy tools in California.
Following the failed 2021 recall attempt against California Governor Gavin Newsom, the state recall process has been criticized for evolving beyond its intended purpose to the point of being overpowered and prone to abuse.
After reviewing the recall’s original intent, we conduct a quantitative analysis of state and local recall attempts in California and compare this to other recall states.
We conclude that the critique is unjustified.
In California and elsewhere, state official recalls are frequently attempted but rarely qualify for the ballot, demonstrating that the existing recall system is an effective filter.
We validate the charge that the recall is primarily a tool of out-party interests, but conclude that this is an intended design feature rather than an unanticipated defect.
We conclude instead that California’s local recall is the better target for reform efforts, given its comparatively easier qualifying requirements, greater use, and higher success rates.
Rather than deviating from its intended purpose, in its 110 years the California state official recall proved to be exactly what its Progressive designers intended: a voter weapon to menace and remove public officials, but one that is difficult to deploy.

***Two Questions in Recall Elections.*** In a recall election, voters are asked two questions: (1) whether the official should be removed from office and (2) who should replace the official if removed from office.
...
### Proposal
***Removes Second Question From Recall Elections.*** Proposition 5 removes the second question—who should replace a recalled official—from a recall election.
This means, in future recall elections, voters would only decide whether to remove an elected official from a state office, not who would replace the official.
***Specifies Steps for Filling Vacant Offices.*** If a state official is recalled, Proposition 5 makes the office of the recalled official vacant.
Except for the office of the Governor, Proposition 5 uses the existing process for filling vacancies to fill the office.
In the case of an office in the state Senate or Assembly, this means that a replacement typically would be elected through a separate special election.
The Governor would choose who would fill a vacancy in any other office (other than office of the Governor).

## Results of Newsom recall certified; 12.8 million total votes cast
On Oct. 22, 2021, California certified the results of the recall election targeting Gov.
Gavin Newsom (D) on Sept. 14. Of the 12.8 million voters who participated in the election, 61.9% voted to retain Newsom, and 38.1% voted to recall.
Forty-six candidates, including nine Democrats and 24 Republicans, ran in the election.
Approximately 7.4 million voters selected a candidate on the second question.
The five candidates to receive the most votes were: radio host Larry Elder (R) with 48.4%, YouTuber Kevin Paffrath (D) with 9.6%, former San Diego Mayor Kevin Faulconer (R) with 8.0%, doctor Brandon Ross (D) with 5.3%, and 2018 gubernatorial candidate John Cox (R) with 4.1%.
...
The recall election presented voters with two questions.
The first asked whether Newsom should be recalled from the office of governor.
The second asked who should succeed Newsom if he is recalled.
A majority vote was required on the first question for the governor to be recalled.
If voters had recalled Newsom, the candidate with the most votes on the second question would have won the election.
Since 1911, there have been 55 attempts to recall a California governor.
The only successful recall campaign was in 2003 when voters recalled then-Gov.
Gray Davis (D).
Arnold Schwarzenegger (R) was elected as Davis' replacement.
In that election, 135 candidates ran, and the winner received 48.6% of the vote.

## Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
### Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

## Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
### Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

# Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
## Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
### Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

And who should replace them?
Under the current system, if the recall is approved, the candidate who receives the most votes on the second question is named the replacement.
Proposition 5 would change this process by eliminating the replacement question, so voters would decide only whether an elected official should be recalled.

# Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
## Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
### Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

***Vacant State Offices.*** State officials may leave office before the end of their term for reasons other than a recall.
For example, they may die or resign.
When this happens, the office becomes vacant.
The process to fill a vacant office varies by office.
Typically, a vacant seat in the Assembly or Senate is filled through a special election called by the Governor.
The Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor when there is a vacancy in the office of the Governor.
Vacancies in other executive offices (for example, the Lieutenant Governor or Attorney General) and the Supreme Court and Courts of Appeal are filled by appointments by the Governor.
***Frequency of Elections.*** Statewide elections in California are scheduled every two years.
In scheduled election years, a primary election is held in either March or June, depending on the year, and a general election is held in November.
In addition to scheduled elections, the state and local governments may call special elections to address specific issues.
For example, the Governor may call a special election to fill a vacant Assembly seat.

As California’s independent oversight agency, the Little Hoover Commission launched a study in 2021-2022 to consider whether the state’s system for recalling state office-holders should be changed, and if so, how.
The Commission concluded that the recall system should be retained, both because it is substantively valuable—voters should be able to fire an elected official mid-term—and because it is overwhelmingly popular with
voters.
Yet substantial changes are needed in 
California’s recall process.
Current recall procedures breed the possibility of an undemocratic outcome, since they allow a replacement candidate to win office while receiving fewer votes than the incumbent.
There is also concern that the recall is subject to potential overuse or abuse.
In its 2022 report, Reforming the Recall, the 
Commission recommends that California make two key changes to its recall system:
◊
Adjust the signature requirement for recalling statewide office-holders from 12 percent of the vote in the last election for the office to 10 percent of registered voters, thereby increasing the number of signatures necessary to initiate a recall election and creating a more stable signature threshold.
◊
Replace the existing two-part recall ballot with a “snap” special election in which the official targeted for recall is placed on the ballot with all replacement candidates.
This would ensure that no official is recalled and replaced by a successor who receives fewer votes.

# Rationality and Rationalistic Choice in the California Recall
## Abstract
The California recall election of 2003 provides an excellent setting for investigating voter rationality and certain forms of sophisticated voting.
In a pre-election telephone survey, 1,500 registered voters were asked to make pairwise comparisons between the major candidates, and their responses were combined to infer preferences.
Individuals’ preference orderings over the major candidates rarely exhibited intransitivity.
The patterns of tactical voting observed in the replacement part of the recall election were consistent with the declining rate hypothesis.
Voters also engaged in ‘hedge voting’ on the recall question itself.
The results suggest that voters’ decisions are ‘rationalistic’: while voters are consistent in forming utility-based preference rankings and choosing on that basis, their voting strategies do not incorporate probability assessments in a realistic, consistent fashion, if at all.

# Rationality and Rationalistic Choice in the California Recall
## Abstract
The California recall election of 2003 provides an excellent setting for investigating voter rationality and certain forms of sophisticated voting.
In a pre-election telephone survey, 1,500 registered voters were asked to make pairwise comparisons between the major candidates, and their responses were combined to infer preferences.
Individuals’ preference orderings over the major candidates rarely exhibited intransitivity.
The patterns of tactical voting observed in the replacement part of the recall election were consistent with the declining rate hypothesis.
Voters also engaged in ‘hedge voting’ on the recall question itself.
The results suggest that voters’ decisions are ‘rationalistic’: while voters are consistent in forming utility-based preference rankings and choosing on that basis, their voting strategies do not incorporate probability assessments in a realistic, consistent fashion, if at all.

## Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
### Additional Titles
Recall Reform, Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment
### Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

- Seven states hold recall elections simultaneously with election for a successor for most offices: Arizona, California, Colorado, Michigan, Nevada, North Dakota and Wisconsin.
- In five states, a recall election is followed by a separate special election for a successor for most state offices: Georgia, Illinois, Louisiana, Minnesota and Rhode Island (state legislature only).
- In eight states, a successor is appointed to fill a vacancy created by a recall election: Alaska, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island (offices of secretary of state, attorney general and state treasurer) and Washington.

##### Recall Reform (2026)
California’s recall election process was designed as a democratic safeguard to hold corrupt or abusive officials accountable.
However, under current law, the recall ballot presents voters with two connected questions: **(1)** Should the official be recalled? and **(2)** If so, who should replace them?
These two questions together create a dangerous loophole.
An elected official can be removed by a narrow majority.
Then, a candidate listed in question #2 can win the office with far less than 50% of the votes cast in the election.
This encourages political actors to target officials they couldn’t defeat in a regular election and to install replacements who lack broad public support.
We saw this dynamic play out during the 2021 gubernatorial recall attempt.
Although voters overwhelmingly rejected the recall by nearly the exact margin as the original gubernatorial election, California taxpayers were forced to pay over **$200 million** for an unnecessary election.
Nearly 70% of California likely voters called the effort a waste of taxpayer money.
Had the recall succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with only about 28% support from recall voters.
Proposition 5 enacts a single, commonsense fix to restore fairness and integrity: **it removes the second question from state recall ballots.**

##### Recall Reform (2026)
California’s recall election process was designed as a democratic safeguard to hold corrupt or abusive officials accountable.
However, under current law, the recall ballot presents voters with two connected questions: **(1)** Should the official be recalled? and **(2)** If so, who should replace them?
These two questions together create a dangerous loophole.
An elected official can be removed by a narrow majority.
Then, a candidate listed in question #2 can win the office with far less than 50% of the votes cast in the election.
This encourages political actors to target officials they couldn’t defeat in a regular election and to install replacements who lack broad public support.
We saw this dynamic play out during the 2021 gubernatorial recall attempt.
Although voters overwhelmingly rejected the recall by nearly the exact margin as the original gubernatorial election, California taxpayers were forced to pay over **$200 million** for an unnecessary election.
Nearly 70% of California likely voters called the effort a waste of taxpayer money.
Had the recall succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with only about 28% support from recall voters.
Proposition 5 enacts a single, commonsense fix to restore fairness and integrity: **it removes the second question from state recall ballots.**

# Your guide to Proposition 5: Big changes to recall elections in California
Proposition 5 would change the way recall elections are conducted in the state by prioritizing voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement.
The ballot measure also would make a major change to gubernatorial recall elections by automatically designating the lieutenant governor as the replacement.

### What will the measure do?
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time.
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to nix that system by first asking voters to choose whether or not to oust an official.
Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date.
In that case, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.

## LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
Under existing law, when a vacancy occurs in the office of Representative to Congress, or in either house of the Legislature, the Governor is required, within 14 days, to issue a proclamation calling a special election to fill the vacancy, as specified.
Existing law requires that such an election be conducted on a Tuesday at least 126 days, but not more than 140 days, following the issuance of the proclamation.
However, existing law also provides that the special election may be consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election, if it is within 180 days of the issuance of the proclamation.
This bill would instead provide that a special election to fill a vacancy in the above-listed offices may be consolidated with any regularly scheduled election that is
within 180 days of the issuance of the proclamation.

## LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
Under existing law, when a vacancy occurs in the office of Representative to Congress, or in either house of the Legislature, the Governor is required, within 14 days, to issue a proclamation calling a special election to fill the vacancy, as specified.
Existing law requires that such an election be conducted on a Tuesday at least 126 days, but not more than 140 days, following the issuance of the proclamation.
However, existing law also provides that the special election may be consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election, if it is within 180 days of the issuance of the proclamation.
This bill would instead provide that a special election to fill a vacancy in the above-listed offices may be consolidated with any regularly scheduled election that is
within 180 days of the issuance of the proclamation.

# What's on California's ballot in the 2026 midterm election? A voter's guide to the statewide races
## Proposition 5: Changes the process for filling vacancies after statewide recall elections
Proposition 5 would change how California fills vacancies when voters recall a statewide elected official.
Under the current system, voters decide whether to remove an official and select a replacement in the same election.
The measure would separate those decisions, generally providing for a subsequent special election or an appointment.

If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.

California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.

Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.

Proposition 5 takes away the ability of Californians to choose their leaders.
Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.

# Proposition 5
## Should successor elections be eliminated from recall elections of state officials?
When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.
## Yes Argument
California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.
In the unsuccessful 2021 recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom, the top replacement candidate received the support of just 28% of voters in the recall election — with millions of voters simply leaving the second question blank.
Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.
## No Argument
Proposition 5 takes away the ability of Californians to choose their leaders.
Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.

# Your last-minute guide to Proposition 5: Changing how recall elections work
## The basics
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time.
Proposition 5 breaks up that process into two parts, prioritizing the voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement.
## The impact
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to change the current recall system.
Under the proposed changes, voters would first be asked to choose whether or not to oust an official.
Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date.
In the case of a special election, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.

The recall, which vested devastating power in the hands of the voters, joined the Progressive agenda rather late.
Its adoption was pioneered by a leading Los Angeles philanthropist, doctor, socialist and Progressive named John Randolph Haynes.
His advocacy led voters in Los Angeles to create the first recall provision in the nation in its 1903 city charter.

## The recall mechanism in California
Like many other US states, Californian democracy provides for the use of the recall mechanism.
Adopted into the Californian constitution in 1911, the recall mechanism is a process by which the electorate can seek the removal of elected public officials before the end of their terms of office.
Prior to 2003, the recall mechanism had been used in California on numerous occasions.
Several local government officials have been recalled, and four state legislators have been recalled, in 1913, 1914 and 1995 (twice).
...
In California, the recall and the vote for a successor to replace the officer should the recall succeed are included on the same ballot.
The officer facing recall is not entitled to stand as a candidate for re-election.
Therefore, if in the first vote the incumbent officer receives the support of more than 50% of the electorate, the recall is defeated and the second vote is irrelevant.
However, if a majority vote to recall the officer, the candidate who receives most votes is elected.

The recall, which vested devastating power in the hands of the voters, joined the Progressive agenda rather late.
Its adoption was pioneered by a leading Los Angeles philanthropist, doctor, socialist and Progressive named John Randolph Haynes.
His advocacy led voters in Los Angeles to create the first recall provision in the nation in its 1903 city charter.

## The recall mechanism in California
Like many other US states, Californian democracy provides for the use of the recall mechanism.
Adopted into the Californian constitution in 1911, the recall mechanism is a process by which the electorate can seek the removal of elected public officials before the end of their terms of office.
Prior to 2003, the recall mechanism had been used in California on numerous occasions.
Several local government officials have been recalled, and four state legislators have been recalled, in 1913, 1914 and 1995 (twice).
...
In California, the recall and the vote for a successor to replace the officer should the recall succeed are included on the same ballot.
The officer facing recall is not entitled to stand as a candidate for re-election.
Therefore, if in the first vote the incumbent officer receives the support of more than 50% of the electorate, the recall is defeated and the second vote is irrelevant.
However, if a majority vote to recall the officer, the candidate who receives most votes is elected.

# Proposition 5
## Should successor elections be eliminated from recall elections of state officials?
When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.
## Yes Argument
California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.
In the unsuccessful 2021 recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom, the top replacement candidate received the support of just 28% of voters in the recall election — with millions of voters simply leaving the second question blank.
Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.
## No Argument
Proposition 5 takes away the ability of Californians to choose their leaders.
Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.
California’s recall system has worked well for more than a century and doesn’t need to be changed.

## Should successor elections be eliminated from recall elections of state officials?
When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.
## Yes Argument
California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.
In the unsuccessful 2021 recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom, the top replacement candidate received the support of just 28% of voters in the recall election — with millions of voters simply leaving the second question blank.
Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.
## No Argument
Proposition 5 takes away the ability of Californians to choose their leaders.
Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.
California’s recall system has worked well for more than a century and doesn’t need to be changed.

#### RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS
California’s recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official.
It should never become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a small fraction of voters.
However, that is exactly what today’s recall rules allow, since the same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets the most votes, even if that’s far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process.
Voters are asked to remove an officer by majority vote, then hand that same office to a replacement chosen by whomever gets the most votes, often in a field crowded with dozens of candidates and with no requirement that the winner reach half the vote.
That’s a loophole that can easily be exploited.
In 2021, had the recall against Governor Newsom succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with the support of just 28% of recall voters, a stark illustration of exactly this problem.
Prop 5 restores the recall to its proper purpose: deciding whether an official should remain in office.
It shuts down that back door with one clean fix: removing the replacement candidate vote from the recall ballot itself.
If a recall succeeds, the vacancy is filled through succession, appointment, or a later election decided by real majority support.
These are the same rules used to fill any other vacancy in state government.

**THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5**
If Prop.
5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled.
If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held.
If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor.

A survey conducted by the Yankelovich Center for Social Science Research at UC San Diego finds wide-ranging support among every demographic, income and party group in California for making “major changes” to California’s recall process.
But it also finds divergence along party lines for which reforms in particular voters would get behind.
...
The survey was conducted during the week of the 2021 recall election with 2,812 respondents reflective of California’s registered voter population.
...
The only reform that was supported by a majority of all respondents was to limit the grounds for recall elections to “concerns about corruption or criminal acts.”
Overall, two-thirds of respondents supported the idea and only 26 percent opposed it.
While there was some partisan divide over this proposal — 76 percent of Democrats in favor compared to 61 percent of Independents and 52 percent of Republicans — it still had majority support in each of these groups.
Other survey findings include that voters back creating a reform commission, but are also open to legislative proposals for reform, and that there is a deep partisan divide over concerns about election fraud that grew even wider after the election.

## No
A NO vote on this measure means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.

Proposition 5 degrades California’s century-old recall process by limiting voters’ right to select a replacement for recalled officials.

# AB-2095 Congressional and legislative vacancies. (2017-2018)
## LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
Under existing law, when a vacancy occurs in the office of Representative to Congress, or in either house of the Legislature, the Governor is required, within 14 days, to issue a proclamation calling a special election to fill the vacancy, as specified.
Existing law requires that such an election be conducted on a Tuesday at least 126 days, but not more than 140 days, following the issuance of the proclamation.
However, existing law also provides that the special election may be consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election, if it is within 180 days of the issuance of the proclamation.
This bill would instead provide that a special election to fill a vacancy in the above-listed offices may be consolidated with any regularly scheduled election that is
within 180 days of the issuance of the proclamation.

### What will the measure do?
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time.
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to nix that system by first asking voters to choose whether or not to oust an official.
Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date.
In that case, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.

# Proposition 5
## Should successor elections be eliminated from recall elections of state officials?
When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.
## Yes Argument
California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.
In the unsuccessful 2021 recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom, the top replacement candidate received the support of just 28% of voters in the recall election — with millions of voters simply leaving the second question blank.
Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.
## No Argument
Proposition 5 takes away the ability of Californians to choose their leaders.
Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.
California’s recall system has worked well for more than a century and doesn’t need to be changed.

# Proposition 5
## Should successor elections be eliminated from recall elections of state officials?
When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.
## Yes Argument
California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.
In the unsuccessful 2021 recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom, the top replacement candidate received the support of just 28% of voters in the recall election — with millions of voters simply leaving the second question blank.
Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.
## No Argument
Proposition 5 takes away the ability of Californians to choose their leaders.
Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.
California’s recall system has worked well for more than a century and doesn’t need to be changed.

# Proposition 5
## Should successor elections be eliminated from recall elections of state officials?
When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.
## Yes Argument
California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.
In the unsuccessful 2021 recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom, the top replacement candidate received the support of just 28% of voters in the recall election — with millions of voters simply leaving the second question blank.
Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.
## No Argument
Proposition 5 takes away the ability of Californians to choose their leaders.
Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.
California’s recall system has worked well for more than a century and doesn’t need to be changed.

When a recall of the Governor is initiated, the Constitution requires the Lieutenant Governor to perform the recall duties of the Governor.
The Constitution requires the Governor to fill vacancies in certain judicial and executive offices by
appointment, as specified.

### Background
***Two Questions in Recall Elections.*** In a recall election, voters are asked two questions: (1) whether the official should be removed from office and (2) who should replace the official if removed from office.
The number of candidates appearing in the second question varies.
For example, there were 135 candidates in the 2003 Governor recall election and 46 candidates in the 2021 Governor recall election.
If a state official is recalled, the person who receives the most votes in the second question assumes the office.

### Proposal
***Removes Second Question From Recall Elections.*** Proposition 5 removes the second question—who should replace a recalled official—from a recall election.

***Specifies Steps for Filling Vacant Offices.*** If a state official is recalled, Proposition 5 makes the office of the recalled official vacant.

# Proposition 5
## Should successor elections be eliminated from recall elections of state officials?
When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.
## Yes Argument
California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.
In the unsuccessful 2021 recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom, the top replacement candidate received the support of just 28% of voters in the recall election — with millions of voters simply leaving the second question blank.
Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.
## No Argument
Proposition 5 takes away the ability of Californians to choose their leaders.
Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.
California’s recall system has worked well for more than a century and doesn’t need to be changed.

## Should successor elections be eliminated from recall elections of state officials?
When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.
## Yes Argument
California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.
In the unsuccessful 2021 recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom, the top replacement candidate received the support of just 28% of voters in the recall election — with millions of voters simply leaving the second question blank.
Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.
## No Argument
Proposition 5 takes away the ability of Californians to choose their leaders.
Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.
California’s recall system has worked well for more than a century and doesn’t need to be changed.

#### * California Constitution - CONS
##### ARTICLE II VOTING, INITIATIVE AND REFERENDUM, AND RECALL [SECTION 1 - SEC. 20]
###### SEC. 15.
(a) An election to determine whether to recall an officer and, if appropriate, to elect a successor shall be called by the Governor and held not less than 60 days nor more than 80 days from the date of certification of sufficient signatures.
(b) A recall election may be conducted within 180 days from the date of certification of sufficient signatures in order that the election may be consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election occurring wholly or partially within the same jurisdiction in which the recall
election is held, if the number of voters eligible to vote at that next regularly scheduled election equal at least 50 percent of all the voters eligible to vote at the recall election.
(c) If the majority vote on the question is to recall, the officer is removed and, if there is a candidate, the candidate who receives a plurality is the successor.
The officer may not be a candidate, nor shall there be any candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d) of Section 16 of Article VI.

# California Proposition 5 (2026): Eliminating the Successor Election in State Officer Recalls
### What California law says now
Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution currently provides that a recall election for a state officer puts two questions on the same ballot:
- Should the officer be recalled?
A majority of votes on this question removes the officer.
- Who should succeed the officer?
The successor is “the candidate who receives a plurality” — no majority required.
- The current text also bars the officer who is the subject of the recall from running as a candidate for successor.

## The impact
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to change the current recall system.
Under the proposed changes, voters would first be asked to choose whether or not to oust an official.
Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date.
In the case of a special election, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.

Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time.

## Opponents argue this initiative strips power from citizens and hands it directly to Sacramento political insiders
...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement.
In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy.
In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.

**Exploring recall election dynamics**

I'm considering how a recall election might play out. It seems that if a majority threshold is not met, support could hinge on 28% of all voters. There are core representation issues to think about. Notably, voters can reject the recall but still opt for a successor, which means the winner could be someone not backed by the overall majority of recall supporters. This situation could feel like a political maneuvering game.**Researching recall dynamics**

I’m assessing the legitimacy of the governor's role versus majority support. I should read the 2021 Commission's analysis to understand the rationale. The user is asking for extensive research, which might include the LAO and contrasting arguments. The PPIC survey won’t be a decisive factor, but I could explore the League of Women Voters' position for a neutral viewpoint. I'll look into the academic article "California's Recall Is Not Overpowered" that discusses recalls and consider its implications. I need to check the bill's hearing history and official criticisms too.**Evaluating the SPUR guide**

The SPUR guide suggests a positive stance, but I need to check if it's truly nonpartisan since it's an urban policy group. It's important to examine pro endorsements to determine if they provide neutral voting advice. I also want to read editorial opposition that raises concerns about the possibility of recalled officials running again, which might be seen as a flaw. Understanding the re-election provisions is key since a public majority's recall doesn't guarantee the official's immediate return; a special election is required instead. The vote could be strategic, allowing voters to express discontent and give another chance for selection.**Analyzing the recall election process**

I think there's a serious issue with how the recall election conflates a referendum on the incumbent with the choice of their successor. This can lead to confusion, as voters may support a candidate while still rejecting the recall, which muddles the message. Separating these questions could clarify things. The current rules allow for direct democracy after a successful recall while ensuring continuity. For governors, the Lieutenant Governor is already separately elected. In the case of legislators, special elections let voters make a choice, even though there's a delay.**Considering recall implications**

It’s interesting that there's only been one successful statewide gubernatorial recall since 2003, which was against Davis. While there are some recall efforts, it seems rational not to amend the constitution for rare occurrences. The Prop 5 proposal could cost millions and lead to a lack of representation due to requiring a special election after a recall. This can empower the governor and potentially allow for partisan influence. Overall, the measure raises substantial concerns about the recall process.**Exploring recall dynamics**

It seems that the current rules around recalls might actually undermine the recall process itself. There’s this fairness issue where a recalled official can't be in the replacement race, but could easily run afterward, potentially reelecting themselves and limiting voter choice. If voters do choose to reelect them, can that count as a legitimate new mandate? The recall rules aim to restore fairness but could still be influenced by partisan politics, especially during special elections. It’s complex!**Analyzing recall elections**

I'm looking at the dynamics of recall elections. The current candidate might secure about 20% support. In a special election with two finalists, that could change.

Now, recalls differ from regular elections since they have two separate votes—it's strategic. If lots of people want to recall the incumbent, they need their preferred candidate to win. However, a candidate could win with just 28% of the vote in a crowded field. This raises questions about fairness. Ranked-choice voting might help clarify preferences, but it also has assumptions about voter turnout.**Examining recall election dynamics**

In a recall election, a majority vote doesn't automatically mean a candidate has widespread support. It's possible for the recall to pass with just over 50%, which complicates how we view the next step. If the support is split among "yes" voters, the replacement might not truly represent the majority's preference.

Voters can pick a successor even if they want the current incumbent to remain, leading to potential mismatches between those who voted for the recall and those supporting a successor. This seems a bit irrational, doesn't it?

Overall, the measure raises substantial concerns about the recall process.**Exploring recall dynamics**\n\nIt seems that the current rules around recalls might actually undermine the recall process itself. 1. California's Recall Is Not Overpowered
https://digitalcommons.law.scu.edu/lawreview/vol62/iss3/1/
# California's Recall Is Not Overpowered
## Abstract
The recall is one of three direct democracy tools in California.
Following the failed 2021 recall attempt against California Governor Gavin Newsom, the state recall process has been criticized for evolving beyond its intended purpose to the point of being overpowered and prone to abuse.
After reviewing the recall’s original intent, we conduct a quantitative analysis of state and local recall attempts in California and compare this to other recall states.
We conclude that the critique is unjustified.
In California and elsewhere, state official recalls are frequently attempted but rarely qualify for the ballot, demonstrating that the existing recall system is an effective filter.
We validate the charge that the recall is primarily a tool of out-party interests, but conclude that this is an intended design feature rather than an unanticipated defect.
We conclude instead that California’s local recall is the better target for reform efforts, given its comparatively easier qualifying requirements, greater use, and higher success rates.
Rather than deviating from its intended purpose, in its 110 years the California state official recall proved to be exactly what its Progressive designers intended: a voter weapon to menace and remove public officials, but one that is difficult to deploy.

CALIFORNIA’S RECALL IS NOT OVERPOWERED 
David A. Carrillo, Joshua Spivak, Natalie Kaliss & Jared 
Madnick* 
The recall is one of three direct democracy tools in California.
Following the failed 2021 recall attempt against California Governor 
Gavin Newsom, the state recall process has been criticized for evolving beyond its intended purpose to the point of being overpowered and prone to abuse.
After reviewing the recall’s original intent, we conduct a quantitative analysis of state and local recall attempts in California and compare this to other recall states.
We conclude that the critique is unjustified.
In California and elsewhere, state official recalls are frequently attempted but rarely qualify for the ballot, demonstrating that the existing recall system is an effective filter.
We validate the charge that the recall is primarily a tool of out-party interests, but conclude that this is an intended design feature rather than an unanticipated defect.
We conclude instead that California’s local recall is the better target for reform efforts, given its comparatively easier qualifying requirements, greater use, and higher success rates.

## The basics
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time.
Proposition 5 breaks up that process into two parts, prioritizing the voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement.
## The impact
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to change the current recall system.
Under the proposed changes, voters would first be asked to choose whether or not to oust an official.
Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date.

# Proposition 5
## Should successor elections be eliminated from recall elections of state officials?
When a state legislator or a statewide official such as the governor faces a recall, voters are asked two questions: Should the lawmaker or official be removed from office?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 would eliminate the successor question.
If a statewide officeholder is recalled, the governor would appoint a replacement, while legislative vacancies would be filled by special election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would serve until another governor is elected.
## Yes Argument
California’s current recall system allows a replacement candidate to take office without winning the support of a majority of voters.
In the unsuccessful 2021 recall of Gov.
Gavin Newsom, the top replacement candidate received the support of just 28% of voters in the recall election — with millions of voters simply leaving the second question blank.
Getting rid of the replacement question keeps the recall election focused on the official facing removal.
## No Argument
Proposition 5 takes away the ability of Californians to choose their leaders.
Voters who recall a governor, attorney general or secretary of state should not have to wait months to pick a replacement — all while the position is filled by someone who was not elected to the job.
California’s recall system has worked well for more than a century and doesn’t need to be changed.
